desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

In one step you may swap two neighbouring nodes of the list. Return the minimum number of steps needed to arrange the list in non-decreasing order. Equal values never have to be swapped with each other.

For example [3,1,2] needs 2 steps and [2,2,1] needs 2 steps. The list can hold thousands of nodes, so simulating bubble sort is too slow.
hints: Each adjacent swap can fix at most one pair of nodes that are in the wrong relative order. Count what must be fixed.
The answer is the number of inversions: pairs of positions i < j with nums[i] > nums[j] (strictly greater, because equal values are never swapped).

Count inversions in O(n log n): either during a merge sort (when you take an element from the right half before the remaining left-half elements, add the number of remaining left elements), or with a Fenwick tree over compressed values while scanning left to right.
editorial: An adjacent swap changes the relative order of exactly one pair of nodes, so it reduces the number of inversions by at most one, and a sorted list has none. Hence at least inv swaps are needed. Bubble sort shows it is enough: whenever the list is unsorted there is an adjacent inverted pair, and swapping it lowers the inversion count by exactly one.

So the answer is the inversion count. Counting with merge sort: when merging two sorted halves, every time the next element comes from the right half, it is smaller than all elements still waiting in the left half, so add that many to the total. This costs O(n log n). The result fits in 32 bits since it is at most n(n-1)/2, about 8 million for n = 4,000.
A Fenwick tree works as well: compress the values to ranks, scan left to right, and for each element add the count of earlier elements with a strictly larger rank.
solution:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = nxt


def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head


def dump(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out


def minAdjacentSwaps(nums):
    head = build(nums)
    vals = []
    cur = head
    while cur:
        vals.append(cur.val)
        cur = cur.next
    n = len(vals)
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(vals)))}
    m = len(rank)
    tree = [0] * (m + 1)
    inv = 0
    for seen, v in enumerate(vals):
        r = rank[v]
        # earlier elements with rank <= r
        s = 0
        i = r
        while i > 0:
            s += tree[i]
            i -= i & -i
        inv += seen - s
        i = r
        while i <= m:
            tree[i] += 1
            i += i & -i
    return inv
